chapter_theme: Kanchanan, come to Puhar for his wife Kayasandikai at the end of her curse, takes Manimekalai in her form for his wife and, seeing her teach Udayakumaran the body's decay by pointing to an old woman, judges the prince her lover; when the prince comes to the hall at midnight Kanchanan kills him, and the pillar goddess tells him that his wife died over the Vindhya, that the prince died by his own former deed, and that the killing will still cling to Kanchanan.

cast.role: the Chola prince of Puhar who pursues Manimekalai
Madhavi's daughter, a Buddhist renunciant, here in Kayasandikai's form
Kayasandikai's vidyadhara husband, who kills the prince
the goddess image on the pillar of the public hall, who speaks

manimekalai:20:1-18.reading: The narrator recalls that the prison, freed of its hellish cruelty by the king's order and Manimekalai's compassion, has become a place of temple, monks' dwelling, kitchen and dining hall; hearing all this, Udayakumaran resolves that, whatever the wise say and however the king rages, he will seize her when she leaves the hall, set her in his golden chariot and hear her learning and her wise old sayings.
manimekalai:20:1-18.nuance: The opening simile (3-4) compares the changed prison to those who, after suffering evil births, reach a good birth through the fruit of their deeds, so the chapter that ends on a killing paid for by deeds opens with deeds as a means of rising. The prince's resolve names the two checks he will override, the wise (மதியோர்) and the king (மன்னவன்), the very sceptre whose order made the hall.
manimekalai:20:1-18.event: Udayakumaran hears that Manimekalai has turned the prison into a house of charity by the king's leave and resolves to carry her off in his chariot.

manimekalai:20:19-32.reading: The prince sets out for the public alms-hall where Manimekalai feeds the hungry; meanwhile Kanchanan, the vidyadhara husband of Kayasandikai, despairing that the twelve years of the sage's curse are over and she has not returned, comes down into the old city, searches its squares, groves, hermitages and halls, and sees the girl relieving people's hunger.
manimekalai:20:19-32.nuance: Kanchanan's lament (22-26) attributes the curse itself to the fruit of an old deed (பழ வினைப் பயத்தான், 23), so even before he acts the chapter frames his story in deeds. What he sees is Manimekalai in Kayasandikai's form, and the narration lets the reader know this while he does not.
manimekalai:20:19-32.event: Udayakumaran heads for the alms-hall while Kanchanan, come to fetch his wife at the end of her curse, searches Puhar and finds Manimekalai, in his wife's form, feeding the hungry.

claims.claim: a sage's curse that falls on a person is the fruit of that person's old deed

manimekalai:20:33-48.reading: Kanchanan greets her fondly, asking whether the gods have ended her elephant-fire hunger now that one bowl in her hand feeds many; unmoved, she leaves him, goes to Udayakumaran, points to a grey-haired old woman and begins to show him, feature by feature, how hair, brow, eyebrows, eyes and nose have turned from their praised likenesses into decay.
manimekalai:20:33-48.nuance: Each feature is first named by its lover's simile (dark sand of the stream, crescent brow, bow, kazhuneer flower, kumizh bud) and then shown in the old woman as its opposite (white sand, wrinkled skin, dried prawn, running water, dripping matter), so the lesson is made out of the love poets' own catalogue. The one who gives it is the desired girl herself, disguised as another man's wife, and the unit opens with that husband's tenderness, which she leaves unanswered.
manimekalai:20:33-48.event: Manimekalai turns away from Kanchanan, who takes her for his wife, and shows Udayakumaran an old woman's face as a lesson on the body.

claims.claim: the beauty praised in a woman's features is changed by age into its opposite

manimekalai:20:49-69.reading: Manimekalai carries the lesson down the old woman's body, teeth, lips, ears, breasts, shoulders, fingers, thighs, calves and feet, each now withered, and ends by telling the prince that he fails to see the deceit those of old set up when they hid the flesh and its smell under flowers, sandal paste, cloth and jewels.
manimekalai:20:49-69.nuance: The closing charge (67-69) blames the deceit not on the woman but on custom, தொல்லோர் வகுத்த வஞ்சம், the dress and ornament handed down by those of old. Her teaching works by showing a living body in time rather than a corpse, and it is the prince's own seeing that she calls at fault (தெரியாய்).
manimekalai:20:49-69.event: Manimekalai finishes showing the prince the old woman's decayed body and tells him its adornment is a deceit.

claims.claim: the adorned body is flesh whose smell is hidden by flowers, paste, cloth and ornament, a deceit established by those of old

manimekalai:20:70-81.reading: When she has spoken thus as the vidyadhara woman, Kanchanan, reading her refusal of his praise, her following of another man, her looking at him as a stranger and her wise talk and smiling eyes for the prince, concludes that the prince is her lover and the reason she stayed on earth, and burning with rage he slips into the hall where she lodges and hides like a snake in its anthill.
manimekalai:20:70-81.nuance: Every sign Kanchanan reads is real (she does ignore him, does go to the prince, does speak to him with care) and every inference is false, because the woman is not his wife and her talk is a lesson against desire. The snake simile (80) begins an image the chapter repeats when he strikes (104-105).
manimekalai:20:70-81.event: Kanchanan decides that the prince is his wife's lover and hides in the hall in anger.
manimekalai:20:70-81.unit_note: End moved from 84 to 81: line 81 (காஞ்சனன் என்னும் கதிர் வாள் விஞ்சையன்) completes the sentence of his hiding, and line 82 begins the prince's part.

manimekalai:20:82-103.reading: The prince, his desire unspent, tells himself that Manimekalai has taken Kayasandikai's form and bowl to bewitch minds and will not leave the stranger she lectured in the hall tonight, so he will come at midnight to learn what she does; with Kama as his companion he leaves the palace when the town sleeps, like a tiger stalking an elephant, and steps slowly into the hall as if entering a cobra's hole, while the vidyadhara waiting there says, 'here he has come to her'.
manimekalai:20:82-103.nuance: The prince also misreads: he suspects her with the stranger (வம்பலன், 88), so each man takes the other for her lover. The narrator's two similes split his part: he goes as a tiger to prey (95) and enters as one going into a hole where a fiery serpent lies (98-99), the hunter already the prey.
manimekalai:20:82-103.event: Udayakumaran, suspecting Manimekalai of a night with a stranger, goes alone at midnight to the hall where Kanchanan lies in wait.
manimekalai:20:82-103.unit_note: Start moved from 85 to 82: line 81 closes Kanchanan's hiding, and the prince's sentence and speech begin at line 82 (ஆங்கு அவள் உரைத்த அரசு இளங் குமரனும்).

manimekalai:20:104-119.reading: Rising like an enraged cobra with poison in its fangs, Kanchanan follows the prince and cuts through his shoulder with his sword, then moves toward the girl to carry 'Kayasandikai' into the sky, when the image of a goddess painted on a pillar of the hall speaks: 'Do not come near, Kanchana! She is Manimekalai in a hidden form; hear how Kayasandikai, freed of her hunger, went: those who fly through the sky do not pass over the Vindhya where the goddess dwells, and any who do are seized by their shadow and put in her belly.'
manimekalai:20:104-119.nuance: The pillar image, which the narrator says a god drew (கடவுள் எழுதிய பாவை, 111), stops the second wrong before it happens and corrects the first too late. Kayasandikai, released by Manimekalai's food to fly home, was lost on the way, so the husband who came for her end of curse kills over a likeness of a wife who no longer lives.
manimekalai:20:104-119.event: Kanchanan kills Udayakumaran with his sword and turns to take Manimekalai, but the pillar image tells him who she is and that his wife died over the Vindhya.

manimekalai:20:120-129.reading: The image finishes: Vindha, the guardian of the Vindhya, took Kayasandikai into her belly; do not grieve, Kanchana; though it was the prince's own ripened former deed that came here and took his life, you did not know that, and you have done a cruel deed that will not leave you either; and the vidyadhara, the hard deed rising in his scorched heart, goes off into the sky.
manimekalai:20:120-129.nuance: The pillar gives two causes at once and keeps both: the prince died by his own ஊழ்வினை (123), and Kanchanan's killing is still his own வெவ் வினை (125) that will cling to him. That he 'did not know' (அறியாய்) excuses nothing; it is the reason he cannot claim to have been fate's instrument. கைம்மை கொள்ளேல் (122) is read here as 'do not take on mourning'; the word can also name rashness, and the line is not certain.
manimekalai:20:120-129.event: The pillar goddess tells Kanchanan that the prince died by his own former deed but that the killing will cling to him, and Kanchanan flies away.

claims.claim: a man may die because his own former deed has ripened and come to take his life
one who kills does a cruel deed that will not leave him, even when the death was the victim's own ripened deed

links.note: The goddess Manimekala warned the prince that a swerving sceptre ruins rain and life and told him to drop his wrongful intent toward one who has taken up tapas; here he resolves to seize her even against the wise and the king.
links.teaches: The prince's death is set up as the end of a refused warning: he was told in advance that his desire for an ascetic was a fault of the sceptre, and he now names the king's anger as one more thing he will override.

links.note: Chithirapathi vowed that she would have the prince carry Manimekalai off in his golden chariot; here the prince himself plans to set her in his golden chariot.
links.teaches: The courtesan mother's plan becomes the prince's own wish in the same image of the golden chariot, so the reader sees the abduction as her design working through him rather than a whim of his alone.

links.note: The sage Viruchikan cursed Kayasandikai to twelve years of burning hunger; Kanchanan comes to Puhar because the twelve years are over and she has not come home.
links.teaches: The twelve-year term set in the curse is what brings the husband to the city on the very days Manimekalai wears his wife's form, so the curse that seemed to end with her cure sets up the killing.

links.note: Freed of her hunger, Kayasandikai told Manimekalai she would go to her city in the sky; the pillar image reveals she was seized over the Vindhya on the way and swallowed by its goddess.
links.teaches: The cure that Manimekalai's bowl gave Kayasandikai did not bring her home: the release she announced ends in a second death, and her husband's search ends in a killing over her likeness.

links.note: At their first meeting in the hall Manimekalai told the prince in words that the human body is a vessel of birth, age, disease and death; here she shows him an old woman's body feature by feature.
links.teaches: Manimekalai moves from stating the doctrine of the suffering body to making the prince look at one, which shows that she treats his desire as a failure of seeing that a statement did not cure.

links.note: The prince praised Manimekalai for setting out 'wise old sayings' (முதுக்குறை முதுமொழி) as part of her allure; Kanchanan sees her setting out the same wise old sayings to the prince and takes it as a lover's talk.
links.teaches: The same words of wisdom are read by both men as courtship, the prince as charm to be won and the husband as proof of betrayal, so her teaching is misheard twice in the way most fatal to each hearer.

links.note: The prince goes at midnight to the hall to take Manimekalai and dies; the next kaathai's report to the king sets his death among those of men who approached chaste wives or ascetic women and died as their evil deed ripened.
links.teaches: The midnight approach is later read as one case in a city's record of such deaths, so the narrative's private intrigue becomes a public precedent that the court uses to explain a prince's death to his father.

links.note: The pillar says the prince died by his own former deed; in the next kaathai the deity tells Manimekalai that deed: in a former birth he cut down a cook with a sword for spoiling a meal for the sage Brahmadharman.
links.teaches: The bare claim of ripened karma is given its content one kaathai later, and the content matches the form of the death, a sword for a sword, so the epic makes its karma traceable rather than merely asserted.

links.note: The quatrain warns men not to desire the spear-eyed woman because she too will stoop and walk with a staff; Manimekalai, the woman desired, points her pursuer to an old woman and shows him eyes and face already changed.
links.teaches: The quatrain's warning against desire is spoken by a man to men about a woman, while the epic puts it in the mouth of the desired woman as her own defence, turning the lesson on aging into a refusal.

gains.a: Manimekalai's demonstration gains a recognized ethical topos, so her act reads as instruction rather than mere evasion.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a case where the warned man ignores the lesson and dies of the desire, which tests what the warning can do.

links.note: The quatrain asks whether spices, flowers in the hair and false finery can remove a foulness the great saw and gave up; Manimekalai says the flowers, paste, cloth and jewels that hide the flesh are a deceit 'those of old' devised.
links.teaches: The quatrain credits the great of the past with seeing through the body's adornment, while the epic blames those of old for building it, so the same disguise is a personal vanity in one and an inherited social custom in the other.

gains.a: The epic's charge against custom gains a parallel in which tradition is on the side of seeing through adornment, which sharpens how unusual its blame of 'those of old' is.
gains.b: The quatrain gains an account of where the false finery comes from, which it treats only as something individuals put on.

links.note: The quatrain's renunciant refuses talk of teeth like jasmine buds and pearls because he has seen fallen teeth and bones in the burning ground; Manimekalai shows teeth once like a row of pearls now loosened in a living mouth.
links.teaches: The quatrain needs the cremation ground to refute the pearl simile, while the epic finds the refutation in a living old woman, so the argument against the body moves from death to aging that every lover can see in the street.

gains.a: Manimekalai's catalogue gains the Naladiyar's frame of rejected similes, showing it answers the praise-poets' language point by point.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a version of its proof that does not wait for death, which widens it from the funeral ground to ordinary life.

links.note: Sivavakkiyar's man, having taken a woman for her form, would cut down any rival who desires her, though his own body will stink and be handed to the cremation keeper; Kanchanan cuts down the prince over a form that is not even his wife's, whose body is already gone.
links.teaches: The epic gives the Siddhar's jealous husband a case where the form (வடிவு) he guards belongs to another woman and his wife's body has already perished, so the jealousy is shown wrong both about whose body it is and about its lasting.

gains.a: Kanchanan's killing gains a general diagnosis: it is jealousy over a body, the most perishable of possessions.
gains.b: The Siddhar's hypothetical gains a narrated case in which the rival is actually killed and the killer's price is named as a deed that clings, beyond the body's decay.

links.note: The quatrain says an old deed finds its doer as a calf finds its mother among many cows; the pillar says the prince's ripened deed came here and took his life, and that Kanchanan's deed will reach him too.
links.teaches: The epic shows the old deed finding its doer across a change of birth and through a stranger's hand, which gives the quatrain's search image a path: the deed reaches the prince by way of another man's mistake.

gains.a: The pillar's statement gains the image of the deed as an active seeker, which explains why a chance misidentification could deliver it.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a case in which one deed's arrival creates a new deed with its own doer, a chain the calf image does not show.

links.note: The couplet says the ruin of evil-doers stays at their feet like a shadow; the pillar tells Kanchanan his cruel deed will not leave him, even though the prince died by his own former deed.
links.teaches: The couplet considers only the doer, while the epic adds that being the instrument of another's ripened karma does not lift the deed from the one who kills, so karma explains the victim's death without excusing the killer.

gains.a: The pillar's warning gains the couplet's image of a consequence that never leaves its doer's feet.
gains.b: The couplet gains a hard case, a killing the victim's own deed called for, in which its rule still holds.

links.note: The couplet says unguarded anger kills the one who has it; Kanchanan's anger, kindled by misread signs, kills the prince, and the pillar then tells him the deed will cling to him.
links.teaches: The epic traces how anger turns on its owner: it begins in a misreading of another's signs, kills someone else first, and returns as a deed that will not leave the angry man, which the couplet states as a single blow.

gains.a: Kanchanan's rage gains the couplet's judgment that the angry man is his own first victim.
gains.b: The couplet gains the route by which anger kills its owner: through the deed done to another and its clinging consequence.

source_issues: Line 23 reads பழப் வினைப் பயத்தான், with a stray ப் after பழ; the sense is பழவினைப் பயத்தான் (the fruit of an old deed).
Line 80 carries a malformed line mark (20-0810) in the source; the line text itself is sound.
Line 91 reads வான்தேர்ப் பாகனைப் மீன், with an unexpected ப் before மீன்.
Line 118 reads போவார் உளர்அனின், which looks corrupt for உளர் எனின் ('if there are any who go').
Chapter 21 of the tool is kaathai 20 (உதயகுமரனைக் காஞ்சனன் வாளால் எறிந்த காதை); unit ids use the kaathai number.
